<!--- Context --->
<!--- 1. Broad field of research --->
Understanding the reasons behind forecast performance is useful for prioritising and interpreting modelling work.
Modellers take many approaches to predicting the course of infectious diseases and achieve a wide range of accuracy as a result.
For example, forecasters vary in their choice of underlying model structure and in the extent to which they adapt a model to the specific forecast target.
However, it has been difficult to evaluate the impact of these choices on realised forecast performance, because comparisons across models also conflate differences in predictive power with differences in target difficulty.

<!--- 2. Narrower field --->

<!--- 3. The one open question answered by the research --->

<!--- Content --->
<!--- 4. Method or approach --->
Here, we develop a model-based approach to adjust for the key sources of variation in predictive difficulty, targeting the controlled direct effect of model structure on performance.
We apply this to a multi-country multi-model forecasting effort conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, in order to assess the influence of models' structure and geographic specificity on forecast accuracy.
We evaluated 181,851 probabilistic predictions from 47 forecasting models participating in the European COVID-19 Forecast Hub between 8 March 2021 and 10 March 2023.
We classified models by structure (agent-based, mechanistic, semi-mechanistic, statistical, or human judgement) and by geographic specificity (forecasts produced for one or multiple locations).
We assessed performance of COVID-19 case and death forecasts, measured as the weighted interval score applied to forecasts and observations normalised to incidence per 100,000 population and log-transformed.
We summarised unadjusted performance descriptively and compared this to adjusted estimates from a generalised additive mixed effects model.
We adjusted for forecast horizon, epidemic trend, dominant variant phase, country location, and individual model variation.

<!--- 5. Executive summary of results --->
Unadjusted estimates suggested differences between model structures, but after adjustment there was little systematic difference in average performance, with no clear difference for case forecasts and only weak differences for death forecasts.

<!--- 6. Expanded detail of results --->
Models forecasting for a single geographic target showed some indication of better performance than those forecasting multiple targets, although these effects were inconclusive with overlapping uncertainty.
We noted substantial residual variation in model performance that our adjustment did not explain.
<!--->
<!--- Conclusion ---> 
<!--- 7. Interpretation of how results answer the one question --->

Valid comparisons of forecast performance require adjusting for the general predictive difficulty of the target.
This work is exploratory.
A fuller causal treatment would pre-specify a directed acyclic graph, examine overlap across model-structure strata, and provide a quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding.
This work was also limited by a small sample of independent models and likely incomplete adjustment for confounding factors.

<!--- 8. How this moves the broader field forward --->
We recommend that multi-model comparisons encourage and document their methodological diversity, and collate detailed structured metadata on model methods alongside numerical predictions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Author summary

- Accurately predicting the spread of infectious disease is essential to supporting public health during outbreaks.
  However, comparing the accuracy of different forecasting models is challenging.
  A model may appear to perform well simply because it happened to forecast easier targets, not because it is more capable.
  Existing evaluations struggle to disentangle the impact of model design choices, such as model structure, or choice of forecast target, from the inherent difficulty of predicting across different outbreak dynamics.
  Our research moves towards a more principled approach to systematically adjusting for common factors affecting epidemiological forecasts, accounting for multi-layered and non-linear effects on predictive difficulty.

- We applied this approach to a dataset of forecasts from 47 different models submitted to the European COVID-19 Forecast Hub.
  We adjusted for variation across epidemic dynamics, forecast horizon, and model-specific effects.
  This allowed us to isolate the impact of model structure on predictive performance, while accounting for geographic specificity and predictive difficulty.

- Our findings suggest that after adjustment, apparent differences in performance between model structures became minimal.
  We could not explain substantial variation in performance between individual models, suggesting the importance of factors beyond those commonly documented, such as team capacity, domain expertise, and model evolution over time.
  Our work highlights the importance of accounting for predictive difficulty when evaluating across a variable set of forecasting models. We provide a framework for more robust evaluations of infectious disease predictions, and suggest what a fuller causal treatment of this question would require.
